title: Operando Attenuated Total Reflectance Far‐Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Analysis at the Cathode/Electrolyte Interface
content:
Operando ATR‐FUV spectroscopy directly probes cathode/electrolyte interfacial chemistry in Li‐ion batteries. Voltage‐dependent species appear at ∼3.9 V vs. Li/Li+, well below the electrolyte oxidation potential, and are assigned to de‐H EC and VC by quantum chemical calculations, revealing a chemically driven dehydrogenation pathway triggered by Li+ deintercalation.








ABSTRACT
Understanding cathode/electrolyte interfacial reactions is critical for improving the stability of high‐voltage Li‐ion batteries; however, the molecular mechanisms governing cathode/electrolyte interphase (CEI) formation remain poorly understood due to the buried and dynamically evolving nature of the interface. Here, we develop an operando attenuated total reflectance far‐ultraviolet (ATR‐FUV) spectroscopic method to directly probe cathode/electrolyte interfacial chemistry during electrochemical cycling. With the aid of principal component analysis, we isolate a voltage‐dependent interfacial spectral component that emerges at ∼3.9 V, well below the onset potential of electrochemical electrolyte oxidation. Supported by quantum chemical calculations, this component is assigned to dehydrogenated ethylene carbonate (de‐H EC) and vinylene carbonate (VC), revealing a chemically driven proton‐abstraction pathway induced by reactive surface oxygen species generated upon Li+ deintercalation. This process recurs upon charging, demonstrating a voltage‐driven yet chemically initiated interfacial reaction distinct from direct electrochemical oxidation. These findings establish operando ATR‐FUV spectroscopy as a powerful tool for resolving transient cathode interfacial chemistry and provide new molecular‐level insights into CEI formation relevant to the design of next‐generation high‐voltage Li‐ion batteries.
journal: Wiley: Angewandte Chemie International Edition: Table of Contents
summary: This is a new operando far-UV ATR method for the buried cathode/electrolyte interface. PCA isolates a voltage-dependent component that appears at about 3.9 V, well below the electrolyte oxidation onset. Calculations assign it to dehydrogenated EC and VC, which points to chemical proton abstraction by reactive surface oxygen after Li+ deintercalation. The assignment depends on calculations, so it is less direct than the method itself.
technique: operando ATR-FUV spectroscopy with PCA and quantum chemical calculations

title:
In Situ Nanoscale
Visualization of Stripping-Induced
Failure Behavior in Aqueous Zinc Batteries
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Aqueous zinc batteries (AZBs) show great promise for large-scale energy storage due to their low cost, intrinsic safety, and environmental compatibility. However, their practical deployment is hindered by dendrite formation, residual zinc (Zn) accumulation, and limited cycle life. Recent studies have identified the stripping process as a critical factor governing battery longevity, yet the underlying failure mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this study, leveraging a fourth-generation synchrotron radiation source, we employed in situ nanoscale X-ray microscopy to visualize the morphological evolution from planar to mossy Zn during cycling at 50 mA cm–2. Combining observations of the entire cycling process with optical flow analysis of the stripping process on different substrates at 1 mA cm–2, we categorize the origins of residual Zn into four distinct pathways: (i) dendrites formed during plating; (ii) dendrites generated by crystallographically selective stripping; (iii) bulky Zn that loses electrical contact during stripping; and (iv) Zn fragments resulting from inward dissolution. Ex-situ XRD and DFT calculations further confirm the preferential dissolution of Zn(100) and Zn(101) over Zn(002). These findings highlight the critical role of the stripping process in AZB failure and demonstrate that minimizing local variations in dissolution behavior through kinetic modulation is one of the keys to achieving complete dissolution and enhancing Zn reversibility.</jats:p>
summary: Operando nano-X-ray microscopy follows Zn plating/stripping, including the planar-to-mossy transition at 50 mA cm-2. Optical flow analysis of stripping classifies residual ("dead") Zn into four origins: plating dendrites, crystallographically selective stripping, electrical isolation, and inward-dissolution fragments. Ex situ XRD and DFT support preferential dissolution of Zn(100) and (101) over (002).
technique: in situ nanoscale transmission X-ray microscopy (4th-gen synchrotron) with optical flow analysis

title: Operando Quantifying Li Plating Processes in Lithium‐Ion Pouch Cells
content:
Dynamic EIS defines a critical Li‐plating areal capacity (qLi) for accurate quantification of Li plating growth. The transmission line model elucidates its physical origin: qLi marks the transition from nucleation‐dominated to growth‐controlled lithium plating. This condition‐dependent parameter decreases with temperature as the nucleation mechanism shifts from 3DP to 2DI. 








ABSTRACT
Lithium‐ion batteries require high reliability and extended lifespan for practical grid storage applications, yet Li plating remains a critical hazard inducing rapid capacity fade and safety risks. The transient and heterogeneous nature of Li plating poses a significant challenge to real‐time quantitative detection. Herein, we define a critical Li‐plating areal capacity (qLi) derived from dynamic electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (DEIS) and establish an operando strategy to accurately quantify Li plating under diverse charging conditions. Validated by operando solid‐state nuclear magnetic resonance (ssNMR)‐DEIS combined measurements, incremental capacity analysis, and mass spectrometry titration (MST), this method demonstrates high reliability, exceptional accuracy (R2 > 0.97), and general validity across different temperatures (0°C–45°C) and battery capacities (4 to 110 mAh). A transmission line model (TLM) elucidates the physical origin of qLi: it corresponds to the critical surface coverage (∼10%, model‐derived) of lithium nuclei on graphite, marking the transition from nucleation‐dominated to growth‐controlled deposition. We further demonstrate that regulating temperature can switch the nucleation mode, thereby significantly altering qLi and the resulting plating characteristics. This study establishes a robust operando quantification platform, enabling early battery warning and adaptive fast charging to suppress excessive Li plating and extend service life in practical cells.
journal: Wiley: Angewandte Chemie International Edition: Table of Contents
summary: Dynamic EIS defines a critical Li-plating areal capacity, validated against operando ssNMR and MS titration in pouch cells (R²>0.97, 0–45 °C). A transmission line model links it to ~10% graphite surface coverage by Li nuclei, the switch from nucleation to growth control, and a temperature-driven change in nucleation mode (3DP to 2DI). The coverage figure is model-derived, not imaged.
technique: operando dynamic EIS with operando solid-state NMR, mass spectrometry titration

title: Hydrogen‐Bonding Order Associated With Radical Delocalization in Layered Organic Cathode Materials
content:
“TAQ” and TAPT share the same pyrazine‐based molecular structure but differ in degree of crystallinity. Combined x‐ray scattering, solid‐state NMR, MicroED, and EPR reveal that “TAQ”'s higher crystallinity and ordered hydrogen‐bonding network are associated with enhanced radical delocalization and conductivity, highlighting structural order as a design principle for organic cathodes. 








ABSTRACT
Organic electrode materials (OEMs) offer a sustainable alternative to inorganic cathodes but typically suffer from low intrinsic electronic conductivity. The material historically reported as bis‐tetraaminobenzoquinone (TAQ) exhibits bulk conductivity two orders of magnitude higher than its close analogue tetraaminophenazine‐tetraone (TAPT), despite their common precursor and nearly identical short‐range structure. This disparity has previously been attributed to distinct molecular skeletons, with TAQ proposed to adopt a piperazine‐type linkage and TAPT a pyrazine ring. Here, combining synchrotron x‐ray scattering, solid‐state 15N and 13C nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), microcrystal electron diffraction (MicroED), continuous‐wave and pulsed electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy, we show that “TAQ” has the same pyrazine‐based molecular structure as TAPT, with no evidence for piperazine core or keto–enol tautomerization. Their key difference lies in synthesis‐dependent degree of crystallinity: “TAQ” exhibits greater long‐range structural coherence and a crystallographically resolved intermolecular hydrogen‐bonding network, whereas TAPT is more disordered. EPR further shows that the higher structural order in “TAQ” is associated with a strongly delocalized π‐spin manifold, while TAPT favors localized or weakly delocalized radicals and stronger local spin coupling. These findings identify degree of crystallinity and hydrogen‐bonding order as key structural features associated with radical delocalization and enhanced conductivity in organic electrodes.
journal: Wiley: Angewandte Chemie International Edition: Table of Contents
summary: Resolves a structural misassignment: "TAQ" is the same pyrazine-based molecule as TAPT, not piperazine, and the conductivity gap of two orders of magnitude comes from crystallinity and ordered hydrogen bonding. EPR links this order to delocalized π-spin. It is a strong multi-technique structural study, but it is on pristine materials, not operando or imaging.
technique: MicroED, solid-state 15N/13C NMR, synchrotron x-ray scattering, pulsed EPR

title: Facet-dependent molecular adsorption modulates zinc anode work function for the favourable orientation of zinc electrocrystallization
content:
Nature Chemistry, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41557-026-02291-7

While additives direct Zn electrocrystallization and impact battery performance, the mechanism remains disputed. Now it has been shown that facet-dependent work function modulation upon additive adsorption governs Fermi-level equilibration and Zn crystallographic texture across 29 additives with 93.1% accuracy, providing an interfacial electronic descriptor for additive screening towards favourable Zn electrodeposition.
summary: Proposes facet-dependent work function change on additive adsorption, via Fermi-level equilibration, as a descriptor of Zn deposit texture. Across 29 additives it predicts orientation with 93.1% accuracy. This is a rare mechanistic, predictive framework for additive screening, though it is not imaging-based and the abstract gives few details.
technique: work function measurements (likely KPFM/UPS), texture analysis across 29 additives

title: Gas Retention in Porous Cathodes Governs Bicarbonate Electrolysis Performance
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Bicarbonate electrolysis offers a direct route for converting captured CO2 into high-value chemicals without energy-intensive CO2 regeneration and compression. However, multiphase transport within liquid-fed porous cathodes remains poorly understood. We found carbon paper and carbon cloth yielded drastically different performance, and further analysis revealed gas retention, i.e., localized and temporary entrapment of internally generated gas within the pore network, as an important transport limitation. Flow pulse and recovery experiments under galvanostatic operations showed largely reversible performance losses, while operando X-ray imaging directly visualized gas retention. Gas retention intensifies with denser electrodes, lower catholyte flow rates, and higher current densities. Guided by these observations, an interdigitated flow field was employed to enhance through-plane convection and gas removal, increasing the maximum formate partial current density to 304 mA cm–2 and enabling 120 h of stable operation. These findings establish gas management as a critical design criterion for bicarbonate electrolyzers.</jats:p>
summary: Operando X-ray imaging directly visualizes gas retention in liquid-fed carbon paper/cloth cathodes during bicarbonate electrolysis, identifying it as a reversible transport limitation. Flow-pulse recovery tests link it to performance, and an interdigitated flow field raised formate partial current density to 304 mA cm–2. This is electrolyzer rather than battery work, but the imaging approach transfers.
technique: operando X-ray imaging (radiography) of gas in porous cathode

title: Direct Evidence of Intermediate Oxygen Species Evolution in Cathode Oxides With Nominally Stable Superstructure
content:
Electrochemical cycling drives oxidized oxygen species in ribbon‐ordered P2 and P3 cathodes from electron holes on O2− and dimerized (O2)n− toward molecular O2, establishing the latter as the inevitable terminal product in cathode oxides with nominally stable superstructures.








ABSTRACT
Anionic redox has fundamentally transformed the traditional approach to developing advanced cathode materials for secondary batteries. Nevertheless, how oxygen anions participate in the redox reaction and evolve during the dynamic intercalation process remains a topic of intense controversy, particularly in prototypical materials featuring a stable superstructure. Herein, we showcase that the oxidized oxygen species at the top of charge of ribbon‐ordered P2‐Na0.6Li0.2Mn0.8O2 continuously evolve during electrochemical cycling—shifting from a mixture of electron holes on O2− and dimerized (O2)n− to a mixture of (O2)n− and molecular O2. The intermediate oxygen species increasingly stabilize as molecular O2 instead of (O2)n−, a process coupled with the expansion of Li‐vacancy clusters and the growth of Mn‐enriched domains. We further demonstrate the same trend in the P3 analogue, which features a more stable ribbon superstructure with a topological “−α−γ−” stacking pattern (“−α−β−” for P2‐Na0.6Li0.2Mn0.8O2), further corroborating that molecular O2 formation is inescapable even when Mn migration is restricted in the pristine structure. Collectively, our results provide direct evidence that electron holes on O2− are unstable upon cycling and identify molecular O2 as the ultimate oxygen‐redox product for cathode oxides with nominally stable superstructure.
journal: Wiley: Angewandte Chemie International Edition: Table of Contents
summary: Tracks oxidised oxygen speciation over cycling in ribbon-ordered P2/P3 Na0.6Li0.2Mn0.8O2. It reports a shift from O2− holes and (O2)n− dimers to trapped molecular O2, coupled with Li-vacancy cluster growth and Mn-rich domain formation. It also shows the same trend in P3, where Mn migration is restricted. Spectroscopic and mostly ex situ, but a clear mechanistic claim.
technique: Likely RIXS / spectroscopy of oxygen redox (ex situ), ribbon-ordered P2/P3 Na cathodes

title: Quantifying the Dissolution of Organic and Inorganic Components in Solid Electrolyte Interphase for Sodium‐Ion Batteries
content:
A quantitative analytical framework combining ion chromatography, electrochemical quartz crystal microbalance, and X‐ray photoelectron spectroscopy reveals that a tetraglyme‐based electrolyte promotes an anion‐enriched solvation shell, yielding a dense, inorganic‐rich solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) on hard carbon anodes. This optimized structure suppresses total SEI dissolution and achieves exceptional cycling stability in sodium‐ion pouch cells.








ABSTRACT
Anode interphase dissolution is a major cause of instability in sodium‐ion batteries (SIBs) because Na‐based solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) compounds are more soluble than their Li analogues. Here, glyme electrolytes with varied chain lengths are used to regulate Na+ solvation structure and clarify its effect on SEI dissolution. A component‐resolved framework combining ion chromatography, mass spectrometry, electrochemical quartz crystal microbalance, and X‐ray photoelectron spectroscopy is developed to quantify the dissolution and retention of organic and inorganic SEI species. This approach determines absolute SEI retention rather than relying on aggregate interphase loss. Compared with the glyme, tetraglyme reduces total SEI dissolution from 75% to 53% and increases the retention of inorganic F‐containing species from 18% to 30%. This improvement arises from an anion‐enriched Na+ solvation shell, which promotes the formation of a thinner, denser, and more inorganic‐rich SEI. Consequently, 1.25 Ah NaNi1/3Fe1/3Mn1/3O2||hard carbon pouch cells using the tetraglyme‐based electrolyte retain 91.2% capacity after 500 cycles and exhibit stable voltage retention during 21‐day aging at 60°C. These results establish a quantitative methodology for distinguishing the dissolution behavior of organic and inorganic SEI components, reveal the role of ether chain length in interphase stability, and provide practical guidance for designing durable SIBs.
journal: Wiley: Angewandte Chemie International Edition: Table of Contents
summary: Quantifies absolute retention of organic and inorganic SEI components on hard carbon, not just aggregate loss. Tetraglyme cuts total SEI dissolution from 75% to 53% and raises retained F-species from 18% to 30%. The anion-rich solvation shell is the proposed cause. The method is useful, but it is not spatially resolved and the electrolyte tuning is partly incremental.
technique: ion chromatography + EQCM + XPS (component-resolved SEI dissolution)
